clinicalPearls: An X-linked disorder caused by mutations in the erythroid/megakaryocytic transcription factor GATA1, presenting in males with thrombocytopenia and variable dyserythropoietic anaemia
The phenotype depends on the specific mutation and can include macrothrombocytopenia, anaemia, and platelet dysfunction
Some mutations produce a beta-thalassaemia-like picture (X-linked thrombocytopenia with thalassaemia)
Bone marrow shows dysplastic megakaryocytes and dyserythropoiesis
GATA1 biology is central to the transient abnormal myelopoiesis and myeloid leukaemia seen in Down syndrome, where acquired somatic GATA1 mutations arise
Platelets may be large with reduced alpha granules and impaired function, contributing to bleeding
Female carriers are usually asymptomatic owing to X-inactivation
Diagnosis is confirmed by GATA1 sequencing alongside marrow and blood findings
reference.pathophysiology: GATA1 is a master transcription factor governing erythroid and megakaryocytic differentiation, acting in partnership with its cofactor FOG1. Germline mutations, often affecting the N-terminal zinc finger or its interaction with FOG1, impair terminal maturation of both lineages, producing dysplastic megakaryocytes with defective platelet production and dyserythropoietic red-cell precursors. Depending on the mutation the anaemia may resemble thalassaemia, and platelet function is frequently impaired. The same pathway is implicated in Down syndrome, where acquired somatic GATA1 mutations in the context of trisomy 21 drive transient abnormal myelopoiesis and myeloid leukaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Other inherited macrothrombocytopenias (for example MYH9-related disorder)
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film assessing platelet size, red-cell indices, and morphology
Bone marrow aspirate showing dysmegakaryopoiesis and dyserythropoiesis
Haemoglobin analysis when a thalassaemia-like phenotype is present
Iron studies where chronic anaemia or transfusion is a factor
redFlags: Severe anaemia or bleeding requiring transfusion support
In a child with Down syndrome, features of transient abnormal myelopoiesis or evolving myeloid leukaemia
Hydrops or severe neonatal anaemia in affected infants
reference.prognosis: Severity is mutation dependent, ranging from mild thrombocytopenia to transfusion-dependent anaemia; with supportive care many patients do well, though the associated Down syndrome myeloid disorders require separate specialist management.
pitfalls: Diagnosing immune thrombocytopenia and giving unnecessary immunosuppression
Misclassifying the anaemia as isolated thalassaemia and missing the underlying transcription-factor defect
Overlooking platelet dysfunction when estimating bleeding risk from the count alone
Not recognising the link between GATA1 and Down syndrome myeloid disease in the relevant clinical context
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
